newsitem.title: UK: Cocoa grinds boosted by demand, new UK capacity.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa grinds boosted by demand, new UK capacity.

text.p: Sharply higher UK and Dutch third quarter cocoa grinds stem as much from a renovated plant put back on stream at a major UK chocolate maker as to buoyant demand, traders and analysts said on Friday.
The total UK grind of 48,855 tonnes, representing a jump of 42 percent, surpassed even the wildest guesses. One industry estimate last week of around 20 percent was conditional.

The news injected fresh optimism to London cocoa futures market, fuelling prices after four consecutive loss days this week. The benchmark March contract was trading 11 stg higher after midday at 996 stg a tonne.
"I don't think anybody was expecting such a big number," said one trader.
Players were already dazzled by the Dutch grind which, according to the cocoa association NCV, rose 16.69 percent to 99,549 tonnes. Analysts had predicted a rise of some 10 percent.
"It's a hell of a grind," commented one trader on the Dutch figure. "It's very, very bullish."

A strong European grind was largely in the cards as cool temperatures had kept the Europeans' appetite for chocolate buoyant this summer. The net effect was also multiplied by exceptionally hot weather last year which had depressed demand. But according to analysts, the flashy UK figure was distorted by old capacity brought back into production last year at Mars -- the top UK producer. The plant had been lying almost idle for a year, undergoing refurbishment.
"The Mars effect has obscured the reality of consumption growth. The grind is not a good measure," said one cocoa buyer at a leading manufacturer.
The Mars factor was also apparent in the second quarter UK grind which had jumped 26 percent from a year ago.
But another startling rise was unlikely next quarter since the Mars plant became operational in the last quarter of 1995.

Industry operators said they could not deny an underlying growth in chocolate demand, but they reckoned the real rise in the grind attributable solely to consumption could not have exceeded 15 percent.

The renovation at the Mars plant is said to have brought the production of cocoa liquor, an intermediate product, to a halt, but it could have been possible to process small amounts for butter, analysts said.
"This shows that last year they probably did nothing, and they have done more this year than they would have done otherwise," said one.
"From now on it will be more of a consumption-based grind rather than capacity-based," said one industry representative.
The strong grind could also be partly explained by possible restocking of products to benefit from attractive butter ratios over beans since last year, cocoa market experts said.
The UK's Biscuit, Cake, Chocolate and Confectionery Alliance (BCCCA) said on Friday the third quarter grind represented an increase of 9.7 percent over the second quarter of 1996.
Cocoa grindings are considered a major indication of consumption.
